Are you assuming here that AI will never, ever code a memory leak? Because I don't think that's the case.

Rust is not the silver bullet its community is trying to meme it into being. Its approach to memory allocation only works in some cases, the rest of the time you're back to refcounting and the potential for leaks.

For AI it's especially bad because they never memorize full codebase context in the way an experienced dev would, so it all becomes very dependent on how your codebase is structured and how you prompt it. GC just eliminates all those bugs and the associated token cost of trying to find and fix them.

hits.author: i2talics
hits.comment_text:
The author is going towards the right solution but their solution has things flipped, and the result feels like a hack. What I would suggest is instead of implementing a trait with a magic type parameter, you should instead solve this by providing an object that dispatches the trait method rather than dispatching it from the target type.

That is, instead of "trait ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> Json }" you should have "trait JsonSerializer<T> { fn to_json(&self, what: &T) -> Json }". Now we can implement "impl JsonSerializer<Date> for ISO8601" and "impl JsonSerializer<Date> for TimestampSeconds".

If this seems a little wordy, realize that actually we've just reimplemented Rust's closures as our own custom trait. So we could just use closures: "JsonSerializer<T>" is the same thing as the trait "Fn(&T) -> Json". This is exactly what serde features, as you can pass in a serializer function rather than using the type itself to look up the behavior[1].

One other place this commonly comes up for me is in comparisons. Some types, like strings, don't have a single universal way to compare them. This means that Ord is insufficient. The solution is to have a "comparator" trait that provides the ordering. Again, this could also just be a closure with two arguments.

[1]: https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#serialize_with
hits.story_title: How to Bypass Rust's Orphan Rule

My bottleneck currently is CI capacity. I've turned every spare computer in my household into a Slurm node so I can run more testing locally to avoid wasting precious CI capacity.

hits.author: jarjoura
hits.comment_text:
Solving coding makes no sense if you're a business that relies on that code.

Every layer of the stack has had decades of eyeballs, research, and actual validation.

Binary machine circuits, run by assembly that has been hand refined from LLVM (and GNU, etc.), generated from higher level languages that have been through so many brilliant engineers over decades that made conscious decisions how their language gets turned into assembly.

I don't need to know what Intel or Apple Silicon circuits do with the C++ or Swift code I write. As an engineer I entrust that these corporations employee other engineers who connect those dots, so that I can focus on C++ or Swift.

Natural Language (already imprecise and clunky) that non-deterministically spits out high level code works because every layer below it is doing the right thing. People love getting LLMs to generate rust because rustc is so crazy strict that LLMs can't cheat.

English on the other hand, every word can have so many meanings and developers who use LLMs to generate things they aren't familiar with, judge models based solely on whether these things can properly capture intent. It's one thing to say we can finally break free of dealing with shoddy, imprecise code, but it's another to say natural language is code.
hits.story_title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it

hits.comment_text:
Agreed, and another point that I haven't seen in the article : 'architect' as a separate software engineering role was a bit of a bad word, even if everybody agreed that architecture was important.

It was mostly because in some companies there was a cast of 'architect' who were seen as above coding, and who mostly delivered out of touch UML diagrams, or ill-fitting data-structure. The core of the issue was that even good programmers would rust and get incapable of understanding the ground truth if the organization discourage them to also be in the implementation side.

Here it's not exactly the same thing with AI, since the loop is dramatically shorter, but the (lack of) feedback issue remains.

I really believe that my added value as a programmer was fundamentaly to evaluate technical tradeoff of the different options to solve a business issues, and them to implement them. Now with Claude code I'm infinitely faster at the implementation part, but I'm also eroding my capacity to evaluate those tradeoff.

Programming is a medium, and you also need to work with it from time to time in order to keep some level of competency. And yet in many companies we are basically forbidden to do that.

I feel that we have been given cars, but have also been forbidden to ever walk again; Sure the car is more efficient most of the time, but there's a an almost-vital reason why we have to do jogging to compensate.
hits.story_title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them

hits.author: cesarb
hits.comment_text:
> Although you can write the or-then-check-zero memcmp in any high level language and it's very unlikely to compile to data-dependent timing unless your compiler is AGI.

No need for "AGI", the compiler just needs to have enough value tracking to know that the value saturates (once a bit is set, it never gets unset), and an heuristic to move the comparison inside the loop when it might allow it to do less loop iterations.

(I wrote a Rust crate to do precisely that kind of "constant time memcmp", and the only truly reliable way to do so without help of the compiler, is by using inline assembly as a "black box" to make a few things invisible to the compiler's optimizer. It was inspired by code in the Linux kernel which did the same thing also using inline assembly as a "black box".)
